chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi, who said:

The Jurist (peace be upon him) said: 'Shortening the prayer (qasr) is valid for two barids, or one barid going and one returning. A barid is six miles, which is two farsakhs. Thus, shortening is for four farsakhs. If a man leaves his home intending to travel twelve miles (which is four farsakhs), then reaches two farsakhs with the intention of returning, or reaches two other farsakhs, he shortens. If he returns to what he intended at the point of reaching two farsakhs and wishes to stay, then full prayer (tamam) is upon him. And if he had shortened, then changed his intention, he must repeat the prayer.'

What this hadith contains, that shortening is for four farsakhs, indicates that the person is free to choose between shortening and full prayer, although the obligation of breaking the fast and shortening the prayer is linked to eight farsakhs.

key_terms.الْبَرِيد: A unit of distance, six miles
key_terms.فَرْسَخ: A unit of distance, two miles

ai.seo_question: What is the required travel distance for shortening prayers in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from the Jurist (peace be upon him) clarifies the jurisprudential threshold for shortening prayers (qasr) at four farsakhs, while noting that the obligation to break the fast (iftar) is linked to a greater distance of eight farsakhs. It further elucidates the dynamic nature of the traveler's status, detailing how changes in intention or duration of stay at the threshold determine whether the prayer remains shortened or becomes full (tamam).
